messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 42
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Farmer
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 76

Mr. Lin is forty-two years old. He lives in a province where the rainy season brings the smell of wet soil and the constant hum of mosquitoes. Every morning before dawn, he walks his rice field, checking the water levels, feeling the mud between his toes. But the field does not feel like his own anymore. It feels like a stage where he performs the motions of his life while his mind plays the same scene over and over.

Two years ago, his daughter Minh was six. She had a fever that started like any other—she was tired, hot, complaining of aches. Mr. Lin’s wife gave her paracetamol. But the fever did not break. On the third day, Minh began vomiting, and her skin turned pale. Mr. Lin carried her to the district hospital, but the doctor said it was serious—dengue hemorrhagic shock. They needed to take her to the city.

He remembers the ambulance ride as a blur of sirens and his own breath. Minh’s lips were dry, her eyes half-closed. He held her hand and prayed to all the spirits he had not spoken to in years. At the city hospital, they put her in intensive care. For four days, Mr. Lin sat on a plastic chair in the hallway, not sleeping, not eating properly, watching the door to her room. He remembers the beeping of machines. He remembers a nurse touching his shoulder and saying, “Her platelets are dropping.” He remembers the exact shade of the fluorescent lights—a sickly yellow—and the way his hands trembled when he signed consent forms.

Minh survived. She made a full recovery. But Mr. Lin did not go home the same man.

Now, when the monsoon starts, he cannot sleep. The sound of rain against the tin roof sends his heart racing. He lies beside his wife, staring at the ceiling, thinking he hears Minh crying, though she sleeps in the next room, healthy and loud with her dreams. He gets up three, four times a night to check her breathing. His wife tells him to stop, to rest, but he cannot. He feels that if he lets his guard down, something terrible will happen again.

At the farm, he used to work with steady patience. Now he finds himself suddenly checking his phone for messages, or stopping mid-step because he thinks he heard a cough from the house—though he is two hundred meters away in the paddy. His neighbors notice he has become short-tempered. When another farmer asks about Minh, he changes the subject quickly, or walks away. He cannot talk about the hospital. He cannot even drive past the clinic in the town center without his chest tightening.

He avoids the news. He avoids stories of illness, even on television. When his wife mentioned that a cousin’s child had a cold, he left the room without a word. He knows he is pushing people away, but every time he tries to think about what happened, his mind goes blank and his throat closes. He cannot remember the details of Minh’s recovery—only that he felt nothing when she was discharged. Numb. He still feels numb most days. Lately, he has started drinking a little at night. Just enough to make the hypervigilance dim.

This morning, he was in the field, repairing an irrigation channel. For a moment he was calm, watching the water flow. Then a bird flew low over his head. He ducked, his heart slamming. He felt the old terror—the same terror he felt in the hospital hallway. He stood there, muddy and shaking, knowing the danger is gone but unable to make his body believe it.
